question: Is the world false (mithyā), and can the Advaita definitions of falsity withstand Vyāsatīrtha's critique? (The Nyāyāmṛta–Advaitasiddhi controversy)

sides.position: The world is real. None of the five Advaita definitions of falsity is coherent; the inferences from 'perceivable', 'insentient' and 'limited' fail; perception, scripture and above all the witness (sākṣin) establish the world's reality, and what the witness establishes is never sublated. The Upaniṣads do not teach an impartite meaning; the flawless Brahman is absolutely different from the flawed souls; liberation is not mere cessation of ignorance, and the liberated are graded.
arguments: the subject 'the world in dispute' and the qualifier 'indeterminable' are unestablished
'perceivable' would make the self false too, or prove what both accept
the witness perceives time and the unsublatedness of what it grasps
the scriptures teach difference ('atat tvam asi'); their great purport is Viṣṇu's supremacy
meditation-born realization pleases the Lord; grace liberates

sides.position: The world is mithyā: not ultimately real, since it is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman, yet not unreal like a hare's horn, since it appears and functions; Madhusūdana defends each of the five definitions of falsity point by point. Perception shows only empirical existence and does not contradict the Upaniṣadic teaching of non-duality, whose purport is the one Brahman; difference belongs to the empirical order; liberation is the cessation of ignorance by knowledge of identity.
arguments: falsity as 'not the locus of either being or non-being', as 'the counterpositive of a negation in all three times in its own substrate', and the other definitions are defended against Vyāsatīrtha
the empirical reality perception grants is compatible with ultimate sublation
the Upaniṣads' purport, known by the six marks, is non-duality
the witness is pure consciousness and does not certify the ultimate reality of objects

historical_debates.name: The Nyāyāmṛta–Advaitasiddhi exchange
historical_debates.date: 16th–18th c. CE (Nyāyāmṛta early 16th c.; Advaitasiddhi 16th c.; Taraṅgiṇī and Laghucandrikā later)
historical_debates.accounts: A written controversy: Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta; Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's point-by-point reply, the Advaitasiddhi; Vyāsa Rāmācārya's Nyāyāmṛta-taraṅgiṇī defending Vyāsatīrtha; Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's Laghucandrikā defending Madhusūdana; further replies on both sides (not all identified in this pass).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition regards its own side as having prevailed; the Mādhva tradition reveres the Nyāyāmṛta and its commentaries, the Advaita tradition the Advaitasiddhi and Laghucandrikā.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: both sides reject the level, standpoint and stage readings.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dvaita rejects all three: difference is 'real in every state, including liberation' (MBTN 1.68–71), the witness shows the world to be unsublated at all times (Anuvyākhyāna 1.4.99–103), and Advaita's two levels of reality are themselves what the Nyāyāmṛta refutes; to call difference 'empirical' is to deny it. Advaita rejects P2 and P4 as reconciliations too: non-duality is not one standpoint among others but the sole reality, and Dvaita's teachings of eternal difference are, for it, errors to be sublated.

candidate_readings.reading: Difference and the world are real at the empirical (vyāvahārika) level, as Advaita itself grants, and non-difference holds at the ultimate level.
Dvaita speaks from the standpoint of the dependent self and its objects, Advaita from the standpoint of the absolute; each is true within its standpoint.
The reality of difference is taught to the seeker; non-difference is realized at the end.

notes: Supplies the Dvaita side of dsp:world-real-or-appearance (U50) as well. The Advaita arguments are summarized from general knowledge of the Advaitasiddhi; U13 should supply text-layer teachings.

question: What does 'tat tvam asi' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) teach — identity of soul and Brahman, or something else?

sides.position: It teaches identity: 'that' (Brahman) and 'you' (the soul) are one consciousness; the words, stripped of their incompatible parts (by implication that drops part and keeps part), point to pure consciousness, as 'this is that Devadatta' identifies one person.
arguments: the ninefold repetition marks it as the Upaniṣad's purport
identity is the fruit that ends sorrow

sides.position: It teaches co-ordinate predication: both words denote Brahman — 'that' as the cause of the world, 'you' as having the individual soul as its body; the soul is a mode of Brahman, one with it as body with embodied self, yet distinct.
arguments: sāmānādhikaraṇya of two words with different grounds referring to one thing
the soul is Brahman's body (śarīra-śarīri-bhāva)

sides.position: It teaches difference: read 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi', 'you are not that', repeated nine times with examples that show difference (the bird tied to its post, honey from many trees, rivers in the sea); or 'aitadātmya' as being under the Lord's control and 'tat tvam asi' as dependence or likeness. Identity contradicts experience ('no one experiences I am omniscient, lord of all') and the conceit of it is the asuras' error.
arguments: experience contradicts identity
no scripture teaches non-difference; all teach difference
the examples illustrate difference
the Nyāyāmṛta refutes the 'impartite meaning' of the sentence

historical_debates.name: Akṣobhya Tīrtha and Vidyāraṇya at Mulbagal
historical_debates.accounts: The Mādhva tradition records a debate on 'tat tvam asi' between Akṣobhya Tīrtha and the Advaitin Vidyāraṇya, with Vedānta Deśika as arbiter, and a verse it ascribes to Deśika: that with the sword of 'tat tvam asi', which separates the Supreme from the soul, Akṣobhya cut down the great forest of Vidyāraṇya.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Mādhva tradition: Akṣobhya prevailed. The Advaita tradition does not accept this account, and the ascription of the verse to Vedānta Deśika is questioned outside the Mādhva tradition.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: all three sides read the same passage with the same exegetical rules and reach opposite purports.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dvaita rejects any reading that makes difference a partial standpoint: the chapter teaches difference and only difference (VTN 1). Advaita holds identity is the sole purport; Viśiṣṭādvaita rejects both unqualified identity and Dvaita's separation of the soul from Brahman's body.

candidate_readings.reading: Identity (of consciousness), inseparability (of body and embodied) and difference (of substance) are each true from a standpoint.
Apply the six marks of purport to the chapter as a whole to decide its purport — a method all three sides accept but apply with opposite results.

notes: A focused exegetical dispute within U50's dsp:souls-one-or-distinct. The Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita sides are summarized from general knowledge; source refs for them are chapter-level.

question: Are the liberated graded in bliss, or equal (or one)?

sides.position: The liberated are graded: each class enjoys a hundredfold more bliss than the one below, up to Brahmā and Vāyu; the five differences and gradation are not lost in liberation.
arguments: scripture lists the hundredfold steps of bliss
fitness is beginningless and unalterable

sides.position: In liberation there is only the one Brahman, whose bliss is without degrees; the graded blisses of scripture (e.g. Taittirīya 2.8) are portions of that bliss experienced under limiting adjuncts, not differences among the liberated.
arguments: liberation is identity with Brahman
gradation belongs to the conditioned state

sides.position: The liberated are equal to Brahman in enjoyment of his bliss, differing from him only in not governing the world; there is no gradation among the released.
arguments: sūtra 4.4.21 speaks of equality in enjoyment
all released souls enjoy the same Brahman

historical_debates.name: Nyāyāmṛta 4 and Advaitasiddhi 4
historical_debates.accounts: The fourth chapters of the two works argue whether the liberated are graded.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each side holds its own view established.

reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dvaita rejects both: gradation is stated doctrinally (not as praise) in classificatory treatises and holds 'always' (MBTN 1.71). Viśiṣṭādvaita and Advaita reject Dvaita's reading of the lists as applying to the liberated.

candidate_readings.reading: Gradation belongs to the relative level, equality or identity to the ultimate.
The hundredfold lists are praise of liberation, not doctrine.

notes: Viśiṣṭādvaita and Advaita sides summarized from general knowledge (sūtra refs at moderate/low confidence).

question: Can every soul eventually be liberated, or are some souls by nature never to be liberated?

sides.position: Souls are of three innate classes: those fit for liberation, those who transmigrate forever, and those fit for eternal blinding darkness; this gradation is beginningless and unalterable, and liberation and darkness are both final.
arguments: the classification is stated in doctrinal treatises (Tattvasaṅkhyāna, Tattvaviveka) and in MBTN 1
fitness is intrinsic; no means can alter it (MBTN 1.95)
scripture speaks of eternal darkness for the enemies of Hari

sides.position: Every soul is in truth Brahman; bondage is ignorance, and any soul that gains the knowledge of identity is liberated; no self is by nature excluded from that knowledge.
arguments: the self of all is one Brahman
liberation is the removal of ignorance, open to all who are qualified

sides.position: All bound souls are capable of liberation through the Lord's grace, won by devotion or surrender; the tradition knows no class of souls eternally excluded from it.
arguments: the Lord's grace is universal in scope
surrender (prapatti) is open to all

reconciliation.tradition_objections: Dvaita rejects both readings: fitness is 'beginningless and endless, and no one can alter it' (MBTN 1.95), and the classification appears in treatises of classification, not in praise or blame. The other schools reject Dvaita's premise of intrinsically unliberable souls.

candidate_readings.reading: The 'classes' describe stages of spiritual maturity, not fixed natures.
The passages on eternal darkness are hortatory warnings (praise and blame).

notes: An analogous Jain doctrine (souls 'incapable of liberation', abhavya) is noted as a term equivalence, not as a side. The Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita positions are summarized from general knowledge.

question: Is Madhva's interpretation of the Brahmasūtras (especially its opening adhikaraṇas) faithful to the sūtras and the Upaniṣads?

sides.position: Appayya Dīkṣita's Madhvatantramukhamardana argues that Madhva's reading of the opening adhikaraṇas departs from the sūtras and the Upaniṣads they summarize.
arguments: examination of Madhva's readings of the first adhikaraṇas

sides.position: Vijayīndra Tīrtha defends Madhva's readings point by point and counter-attacks the Advaita readings.
arguments: Madhva's readings follow the sūtras' words and the sadāgamas they rest on

historical_debates.name: Appayya Dīkṣita and Vijayīndra Tīrtha
historical_debates.accounts: A written exchange (and, in the Mādhva tradition's account, debates in the Tanjore–Kumbhakonam region); details beyond the titles were not verified.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition regards its champion as having prevailed.

reconciliation.tradition_objections: Both sides claim the sūtras' purport; neither accepts the other's reading as a complementary view.

candidate_readings.reading: Decide the sūtras' purport by the six marks — accepted by both, applied differently.

notes: Titles recalled; contents summarized at low confidence. Listed as a gap to verify.

question: Are the scriptural passages Madhva quotes from works not otherwise known (e.g. 'Bhāllaveya śruti', 'Brahmatarka', 'Paramaśruti') authentic scripture?

sides.position: They are genuine scripture — quoted from Vedic recensions, Pañcarātra texts and Purāṇa portions available to Madhva but now rare or lost; Madhva, as Vāyu's avatāra who received the Vedas' meaning from Vyāsa, had access to them.
arguments: many old texts have been lost
Madhva's authority as Vāyu's avatāra and Vyāsa's disciple

sides.position: Critics of Madhva have questioned the authority of quotations that cannot be traced in known texts and declined to accept them as scripture.
arguments: the passages are not found in the known recensions

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled — a question of textual history, outside the reconciliation principles.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Dvaita tradition rejects the critics' premise; the critics reject the tradition's appeal to lost texts. This is a historical question about sources and no reconciliation principle applies.

notes: Scholarly metadata (labelled, not a side): some modern scholars (e.g. R. Mesquita) have argued that Madhva composed some of these passages; others (e.g. B. N. K. Sharma) defend their authenticity. Which classical opponent first raised the charge was not verified.
